lines.text: Your exam starts at 9 o'clock, on the other side of the city, 40 minutes by bus.
You squeeze your eyes shut, picture the school hallway, and pop!
You're standing in the hallway, still holding your toothbrush.
Where, where did you come from?
You walk into the exam at 8.59 and 40 seconds.
One sock, toothbrush in your pocket, best grade in the class.
That's the last normal morning you'll ever have.
In one week, you'll eat breakfast in Paris and be home before your parents wake up.
In three weeks, a government agent will know your name.
And in 40 days, you'll make one jump in front of the whole world.
A jump you can never take back.
So, what if you could teleport?
First, you need to figure out how this thing works.
You spend the whole weekend testing in your bedroom.
Sam, your best friend, holds a stopwatch and a notebook.
Big jumps only work to places you've seen with your own eyes.
You stare at a picture of a beach in the Maldives for 10 minutes.
You land in your own shower, fully dressed.
Short jumps, under about 50 kilometers, you can do blind.
You just face a direction and go.
You land roughly where you aimed, give or take a few hundred meters.
Whatever you're touching comes with you.
Your backpack, your phone, Sam's arm.
Sam lands in the kitchen, looks at you, and throws up into the sink.
Next time, he says, warn me.
Rule four is the one that almost kills you.
Saturday afternoon, you try your first long jump, 80 kilometers, to the lake where your grandpa used to fish.
Like someone shoved you off a moving bike.
you stumble three steps and fall face first into the water.
Here's what happened, and this part is real.
At the equator, the ground under your feet is moving at about 1,670 kilometers per hour, faster than the speed of sound.
You don't feel it because everything moves with you.
The air, the house, the chips.
But every spot on the planet moves at a slightly different speed in a slightly different direction.
When you teleport, you keep the speed of the place you left, so you arrive moving wrong.
Jump straight from your bedroom to Paris and you'd hit the ground at around 250 kilometers per hour, like falling out of a race car.
So you learn to hop, 50 kilometers at a time, each landing a small stumble.
Let the ground catch you, then jump again.
Sam does the math on a napkin.
Paris is about a thousand kilometers.
If you hop every two seconds, 40 seconds, 40 seconds, Sam says, your knees are going to hate you.
And at first, your life just gets ridiculously convenient.
Most people spend almost an hour a day commuting.
Add that up, and it's about 10 full days a year staring at the back of someone else's car.
You forget your charger at home?
Your favorite pizza place is in Naples?
Your pizza is still hot when you get it home.
The guy at the counter sees you every Friday at 7.
You sleep 40 minutes longer every single morning.
Your mom thinks you've finally got your life together.
Your first trip to Paris takes 20 blind hops.
You land in a cow field, a parking lot, a stranger's wedding right next to the cake.
But once you've stood on that bridge over the river, it's yours forever.
Now, Paris is one memory away.
Your weekends start to look like this.
A croissant in Paris at 8 a.m.
Back in bed before anyone notices.
Each one is a dot in your head that never fades.
You watch the sunset from a rooftop in Paris.
Then you hop home and watch it again an hour later from your own roof.
There's just one thing nobody warned you about.
Your body has a clock inside it, and it doesn't care how you travel.
Pop between time zones every night, and your brain stops knowing what day it is.
You fall asleep in math class.
In 2017, Chinese scientists teleported the quantum state of a single photon from the ground to a satellite more than 1,000 kilometers away.
Not a person, not even a whole particle, just its information.
You just teleported a large pepperoni pizza.
But every superpower has a price.
You've been to 11 countries this month.
You pop onto that Paris bridge at noon, right behind a girl filming her boyfriend's proposal.
By Monday, the clip has 14 million views.
Hoodie guy appears out of thin air.
Half the comments say it's fake.
The other half are trying to figure out who you are.
Lots of people have that hoodie.
It has my ketchup stain on it.
Three weeks after your first jump, there's a knock at the door.
A woman in a gray suit.
And yet you were filmed in Paris on Saturday, and 40 minutes later, you bought a pizza in Naples.
She slides a card across the kitchen table.
Nothing is locked for someone like you.
People will pay anything for that.
And some of them will do much worse than pay.
Every vault in the world has a door.
You could be a billionaire by Friday.
But every dollar you take belongs to somebody.
And if you say yes, you're not a person anymore.
You're not the only one who watched that video.
You jump only from bathrooms and back alleys.
You check over your shoulder every time.
You can go anywhere on Earth, and suddenly, there's nowhere you feel safe.
So here's my question for you.
If you could teleport anywhere right now, where would you go first?
The only place you still go openly is the care home.
Your grandma Rosa lives there, 900 kilometers away.
Your family used to visit twice a year.
Most days, she doesn't remember your name.
She calls you the nice boy.
But there's one thing she never forgets.
She grew up in a tiny village on a cliff above the sea in the south of Italy.
Behind her house stood a lemon tree her father planted the year she was born.
She left at 17 and never went back.
The lemons were as big as your fist, she says.
I'd give anything to smell that tree one more time.
The doctors say she's too weak to travel.
An airport, a plane, hours in a car.
She doesn't have much time, the nurse tells your mom in the hallway.
You could hop blind, but blind hops land you a few hundred meters off.
In a village on a cliff, a few hundred meters off means the sea.
With her, every landing has to be perfect.
You need to see that tree with your own eyes.
So, you do it the slow way.
Two trains, a bus, and a ferry.
You climb a hundred steps up a cliff and ask a very confused old man in terrible Italian, Rosa?
He takes you behind an empty house.
Covered in lemons as big as your fist.
You stand there for ten minutes, memorizing it.
Then, you go back for her.
You tell the nurse you're taking Grandma for a walk in the garden.
Behind the hedge, you take her hand.
For her, you make the hops tiny.
Barely a breath of wind at every landing.
You hold her hand the whole way.
Warm sun, salty air, and the smell of lemons.
She doesn't say anything for a long time.
She walks up to the tree, slowly, and puts her hand on the trunk like she's touching an old friend.
She picks one lemon and holds it under her nose.
Then she turns to you and says, Nico, my Nico, how did you do this?
For the first time in a year, she remembers your name.
She tells you stories you've never heard.
About her father, about the sea, about the boy she kissed under this tree, who was definitely not grandpa.
Don't tell your mother, she laughs.
That night, she sleeps with the lemon on her pillow.
The nurse can't figure out where it came from.
But for the first time, it feels like this power was made for something.
You're at home doing homework when the TV turns red.
The dam above a small valley town has cracked.
The river is rising faster than anyone expected.
Helicopters can't fly in this wind.
Dozens of people are stuck on rooftops, and the water is still coming up.
You hop through it every Sunday on the way to Grandma.
He looks at the TV, then at you.
If you go, everyone will know.
If you go, there's no more hiding.
This is the jump you can never take back.
On the screen, a little girl on a roof is waving a red jacket at a helicopter that can't land.
The roof is shaking under your feet.
You grab the girl and her dad.
An old man on top of a car.
Every jump, your knees hit the ground.
On jump 47, the last roof goes under the water.
You lie on the floor of the school gym, soaking wet, staring at the ceiling.
Everyone in that gym is filming you.
By morning, the whole planet knows your face.
Two days later, you go to see grandma.
There are reporters outside your house, so you hop straight into her room.
Soaking wet, carrying a little girl in a red jacket.
The anchor says, Who is the teleporting teenager?
Grandma points at the screen, then at you, and she smiles.
That's my Nico, she tells the nurse.
He takes me to see lemons.
The nurse laughs and pats her hand.
That evening, Agent Hale is waiting in your kitchen again.
This time, she isn't sliding a card across the table.
She's holding a newspaper with your face on it.
You know what you did, she says.
You made yourself impossible to hide and impossible to use.
Anyone who comes after you now, the whole world will be watching.
Then she does something you've never seen her do.
You sit alone in the kitchen.
Then the air in front of you ripples.
A girl about your age is standing in your kitchen.
She looks around like she owns the place.
So, you're the one from the news.
Someone who's been teleporting for six years.
And trust me, you're doing it all wrong.
And on the table, right where she was standing, there's a lemon.
If you could teleport, would you stay invisible to keep your normal life, or would you jump, even if it meant the whole world would know your name forever?
Tell me in the comments, and if you want to know who that girl is, hit like and subscribe.
